clue.text: Buggy sort of cabriolet is got out

indicators.note: out signals letters knocked out of their order and rearranged, as in 'put out'

explanation.surface: A carriage-loving description of someone shaken out of a cabriolet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Buggy' looks like a carriage (a buggy, like a cabriolet), but 'Buggy sort' is someone concerned with bugs, i.e. germs. 'out' rearranges CABRIOLET IS GOT.
explanation.definitionFit: A scientist who studies bacteria deals with bugs in the germ sense, so is a playful bug-minded type.

clue.text: Check books of a university on spoken French

parts.note: dit is French for 'said', i.e. spoken

explanation.surface: An inspection of a university's library holdings in spoken French.
explanation.definitionFit: Inspecting a firm's accounts is the formal financial examination known by this term.

clue.text: Inn well known, thanks to poet

definitions.text: Inn well known, thanks to poet

parts.words: Inn well known, thanks to poet
parts.note: the Southwark inn where Chaucer's pilgrims gather in The Canterbury Tales, famous because the poet set his opening there

explanation.surface: A pub that owes its fame to a poet.
explanation.walkthrough: Chaucer's Canterbury pilgrims set out from this real inn in Southwark, London; the word also names a herald's short sleeveless coat.
explanation.definitionFit: The inn named in Chaucer's General Prologue is the one the poet made famous.

clue.text: Hood supporting out spoken petition that has no ringleader

indicators.note: in a down clue the second piece sits below and so holds up the first

parts.note: read as 'outspoken': round can mean plain-spoken or blunt, as in a round rebuke
Robin Hood, the outlaw of English legend

explanation.surface: An outlaw backing a frank petition signed with no leader.
explanation.walkthrough: The print splits 'outspoken'; 'round' in the sense of candid. A round robin was signed in a circle so no name headed it.
explanation.definitionFit: A round-robin petition has signatures in a ring so that nobody can be picked out as instigator.

clue.text: What bookies offer is not evens!

definitions.meaning: bookmakers quote prices such as 5-1 for a bet
uneven numbers, such as 1, 3, 5, are not even

explanation.surface: A remark that bookmakers never give an even-money price.
explanation.definitionFit: Betting prices and uneven numbers share one plural word, the betting sense and the arithmetic sense.

clue.text: Pub taking no part in novelty welcome

indicators.note: the pub's letters play no part, so they are removed from the longer word

parts.note: a novelty is something new, an innovation

explanation.surface: A pub refusing to join in some new fad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taking no part in' strips INN from INNOVATION, leaving the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: A rousing round of applause is a warm greeting, so a welcome in noun form.

clue.text: Short intro at home, so essential

indicators.note: short means cut down, so the last letter of the following word is dropped

explanation.surface: A brief introduction given at home, and so vital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Short' lops the O off INTRO to give INTR.
explanation.definitionFit: Something inherent belongs to a thing's very nature, which is what essential means here.

clue.text: Very panicky, restrict kroner in exchange

indicators.note: exchanged letters swap places, hinted at by the currency exchange of the surface

explanation.surface: Someone panicking about restrictions on swapping Scandinavian currency.
explanation.definitionFit: Being stricken with terror is being overcome by fear, so extremely panicky.

clue.text: Mark, constitutional representative

definitions.meaning: a mark is a distinguishing feature or trait
belonging to one's constitution or nature, inherent
typical of a class or person

explanation.surface: A list of words describing a political delegate.
explanation.definitionFit: As noun it means a distinguishing trait; as adjective it means inherent in nature and also typical.

clue.text: Skin pale, being ultra-conservative

parts.note: a hide is an animal's skin
a pale is a boundary or limit, as in 'beyond the pale', and bound means the same

explanation.surface: A pale-skinned person who is very old-fashioned.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone bound by narrow habits refuses change, so they are deeply reactionary.

clue.text: Change in usual terms

indicators.note: in tells us the letters sit inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: A shift in standard contract terms.
explanation.definitionFit: To modify something is to make it different, a straight synonym for the verb.

clue.text: How Falstaff gave up work and hit the sack?

definitions.text: How Falstaff gave up work and hit the sack?

parts.words: How Falstaff gave up work and hit the sack?
parts.note: Falstaff, Shakespeare's drinker of sack (sherry), stops working and goes to bed, and 'hit the sack' also suggests he was weary once more

explanation.surface: A joke about Shakespeare's fat knight quitting work and going to bed.
explanation.walkthrough: The word means both 'gave up work' and 'went to bed', and split as RE-TIRED it means 'tired again'; Falstaff's favourite drink, sack, adds the pun.
explanation.definitionFit: Stopping work for good and going to bed are both senses of the same past-tense verb.

clue.text: Romantic drive? Look around in the same place

indicators.note: the first word's letters go around the second

parts.note: lo is an old word for look
ibid., short for Latin ibidem, means in the same place

explanation.surface: A romantic outing, looking around the same spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Romantic drive' sounds like a car trip, but it is sexual urge; 'around' is the container signal. 'Ibid.' is the footnote abbreviation for Latin ibidem.
explanation.definitionFit: Sexual desire is the psychological drive behind romance, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Firm belief in Jane Austen's work

definitions.meaning: a conviction or creed held firmly
the title of Jane Austen's last completed novel (1817)

explanation.surface: A strong conviction found within a novel by Jane Austen.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means a settled conviction and is also the title of an Austen novel.

clue.text: Christian Egyptian collared, we hear

indicators.note: says the next word is heard, not read, so it is said aloud

parts.note: copped is slang for arrested or collared

explanation.surface: An Egyptian Christian arrested, according to rumour.
explanation.definitionFit: Members of Egypt's ancient native Christian church are called by this name.

clue.text: No major work, making tea with hot water appliance

parts.note: a pot is what tea is made in, so 'making tea' suggests the pot

explanation.surface: A minor creative effort, produced while brewing tea with the boiler.
explanation.definitionFit: A potboiler is a hack piece written just to earn money, hardly a masterpiece.

clue.text: Denim sorts, possibly, these avant-garde painters

indicators.note: possibly says the letters could be arranged otherwise

explanation.surface: Artists of the new movement characterised as types who wear denim.
explanation.definitionFit: Artists breaking with tradition in the early twentieth century are grouped under this term.

clue.text: Fan sustain the circulation?

indicators.note: circulating letters move around into a new order

explanation.surface: A supporter who keeps blood circulating, or keeps a newspaper's circulation up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fan' looks like a device to circulate air, but it is a devotee.
explanation.definitionFit: A fan is an ardent devotee, someone keen on a hobby or team.

clue.text: Heedless of a conflict in a French setting

indicators.note: the French word acts as a setting into which the other pieces are placed

explanation.surface: Ignorant of a war fought in France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'setting' is the container signal; the 'in' before 'a French' is a link. UNE is French for 'a'.
explanation.definitionFit: Being heedless of something means not noticing it, i.e. not knowing about it.

clue.text: Evidence of earlier damage in southern saloon

parts.note: a saloon is a type of car

explanation.surface: A dent in a southern saloon car showing past harm.
explanation.definitionFit: A mark left by a healed wound is visible proof of past injury.

clue.text: Old injury from wild she-cat

indicators.note: wild says the letters run loose into a new order

explanation.surface: A long-ago wound inflicted by a feral female cat.
explanation.definitionFit: As an archaic noun the word meant harm or hurt, kept today in 'unscathed'.

clue.text: Is nothing secure on this map line?

parts.note: O, the figure zero, means nothing
to bar a door is to secure it

explanation.surface: Asking whether nothing on this weather chart line is safe.
explanation.definitionFit: On a weather map a line joining points of equal pressure is called by this name.

clue.text: Hermit vinegary about society

indicators.note: the first word's letters go around the second

explanation.surface: A recluse who is sour about society.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone living in strict self-denial, such as a hermit, is a classic example of this.

clue.text: Cordial, fashion in clubs originally

parts.note: ton is an old word for fashion or style

indicators.note: originally points to the opening letters of the words that follow

explanation.surface: A soft drink in fashion at nightclubs.
explanation.definitionFit: A cordial is a reviving drink, and so is a tonic, as in a pick-me-up.

clue.text: Spring in meadow, with first of primroses

indicators.note: first of picks out the opening letter of the word after it

explanation.surface: Springtime in a meadow, with primroses appearing first.
explanation.definitionFit: To spring is to jump, so the noun spring and the noun meaning a jump are synonyms.

clue.text: A Trollope, it is said, retired here in the US

indicators.note: retired means drawn back, so the letters run in reverse

parts.note: Trollope (the novelist) said aloud is 'trollop', another word for a slut

explanation.surface: Anthony Trollope supposedly retired to an American city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retired' turns A SLUT round. The name Trollope, the Victorian novelist, sounds like trollop, a loose woman.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is an Oklahoma city, a place in the US, so 'here in the US' fits.

clue.text: Being in the world

definitions.meaning: the state of being alive or real
all that exists, the whole of creation

explanation.surface: A being living in the world.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun means both the fact of being and everything that is, the world.

clue.text: Agreement in writing

definitions.meaning: a match or likeness between things

explanation.surface: A contract set down on paper.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both agreement or match and the letters people write to each other.
